On Ramchandra Ray’s escape night, Sitaram is still bound by the Maharaj’s orders: he opens the door but refuses to fight Udayaditya, asking instead to be disarmed and tied so he will not be punished. Udayaditya overpowers and binds him, then escapes. On Udayaditya’s escape night, the roles reverse: Sitaram himself opens the prison, tells Udayaditya to come out because of the fire, physically helps him escape, and guides him to safety.

Pratapaditya initially planned for two Pathan men to waylay Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali on his journey to Jessore and kill him. When that failed, Basanta Ray was finally killed by Abdul, who carried out Pratapaditya’s signed death order by striking him with a sword.

In the inner quarters, disguised as a middle-aged palace woman; and later in the palace chamber before the king, where he appeared as the jester Ramai Bhand—not in another disguise—and Rammohan threw him out.
Rukmini, posing as Mangala, secretly prepared and administered poison to Surma, causing her death before she could depart.

Her refusal leads Ramchandra Ray to remarry in revenge, leaving Vibha without a place in her husband’s palace; when she finally arrives, she finds the wedding underway and her hopes of happiness shattered.

Rukmini gives the ring bearing Udayaditya’s engraved seal to Sitaram, who uses it to stamp a forged petition supposedly written by Udayaditya accusing Pratapaditya of treason. Bhagavat presents the petition to Pratapaditya as evidence that Udayaditya is plotting against him, prompting Pratapaditya to order Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Ramchandra’s escape exposed the palace guards’ failure—especially Sitaram and Bhagavat—and they were dismissed, leaving their families destitute. Udayaditya first supported them, and when Pratapaditya forbade this, Surma secretly continued sending them stipends. Once Pratap learned of Surma’s disobedience, he ordered her sent to her father’s house, effectively exiling her.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s profound loneliness and grief over the disappearance of the people he loved: everything once filling his life has vanished, leaving him with only emptiness and no one for whom to sing or live joyfully.

He sings it first alone in Raigarh at sunset, mourning his absent loved ones and Udayaditya’s imprisonment; he sings it again in Jessore while standing before the now-silent room of Surma, with Vibha beside him, confronting the desolation of the broken household.

Rukmini failed to prevent Udayaditya’s escape when Sitaram’s men stopped her at the canal and she leapt into the water. She then told Pratapaditya that Udayaditya had fled with Basanta Ray and that Sitaram had arranged it. This provoked Pratapaditya to send Muktiyar Khan with orders to seize Udayaditya and execute Basanta Ray if he was found. Rukmini later located Udayaditya at Raigarh, enabling his capture; Muktiyar’s soldiers then entered the fort and carried out the death order, killing Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra coldly and dismissively, offering little welcome and treating him as an unimportant petitioner rather than a royal son-in-law. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra reverses the humiliation: he allows Pratapaditya to be mocked as an upstart of only two generations whose family once depended on Ramchandra’s ancestors for royal recognition, presenting himself as socially and dynastically superior.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles near Jessore, where she ingratiates herself with the palace servants and poses as a widow skilled in tantra, medicine, and magic. Through the Rajmahishi, she prepares a poisoned “medicine” meant to destroy Surma without awakening Udayaditya’s pity. Surma takes it and dies, and Rukmini later reappears in Udayaditya’s chamber, deceitfully claiming that he ruined her and demanding his love.

Udayaditya’s early lament grows from his misery at being treated as an incapable heir rather than a son, and from his wish to escape the burdens, scrutiny, and humiliations of royal life. Though Surma gives him confidence and strength, he eventually concludes that his weakness has brought ruin upon others. After returning to Jessore as a prisoner, he admits to Pratapaditya that he is unworthy of the kingdom and asks to be released from the throne. He then formally swears before Ma-Kali that he will never rule Jessore, accept any part of its kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter, naming Samaraditya as heir and choosing exile in Kashi instead.

Nayanchand, afraid of the consequences if Pratapaditya received the letter, handed it to the Mahishi instead of delivering it. Unable to tell Vibha or risk showing it to the Maharaj, she took it to Basanta Ray for advice. After reading Ramchandra Ray’s spiteful declaration that he had renounced Vibha and would not have her sent to Chandradwip, Basanta Ray mistakenly assumed it had been written only in anger and that Ramchandra’s resentment would disappear if Vibha returned. He therefore advised the Mahishi to conceal the real contents and announce that Ramchandra had written requesting Vibha’s return. The Mahishi accepted this interpretation, and Vibha was told the false, comforting version, believing that her husband understood and still loved her.

Pratapaditya orders the canal beside the palace to be blocked with large sal-wood logs, assuming Ramchandra’s boat will be trapped there. However, Rammohan and his companions pull the boat up and over the logs, escaping before the guards can organize a pursuit. The guards’ delayed chase—compounded by their failure to find ammunition and the boatman’s distractions—allows Ramchandra to get away.

Basanta Ray’s sitar, once his constant companion and source of shared joy, becomes a symbol of his emotional collapse as Udayaditya is taken from him. At the farewell, he tries to play furiously, but tears and grief make it impossible, so he leaves the sitar behind, saying he will never play it again. Later, separated from Udayaditya and learning that he is imprisoned, Basanta Ray says the sitar’s strings have broken and cannot be tuned. Its silence reflects his belief that those he played and sang for are gone, leaving him alone and without the joy or purpose music once gave him.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for boldly intervening in his oppressed subjects’ affairs, even against Pratapaditya’s wishes and without regard for the consequences. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya paralyzes him: he abandons plans to stop oppression, flees from a beaten subject, and cannot bring himself to provide financial help to those in hardship.
He sets fire to the prison as a diversion, then opens Udayaditya’s cell, carries him out, and leads him to safety.

First, he ties thick sheets into a rope, fastens it to a palace-roof pillar, carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down the rope, then lowers him into the waiting boat and jumps down after him.

Later, after throwing Ramai Bhand out by the scruff of his neck, Rammohan lifts the unconscious Vibha, carries her from the palace, and places her in a palanquin by the gate before returning to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately dressed by the Mahishi in eight thick gold bangles, a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an imposed, carefully styled coiffure. Radiantly happy and unable to conceal her joy, she appears as a richly adorned princess preparing to receive her husband. In Chandradwip, by contrast, she abandons all royal display: refusing a palanquin, she dresses as a common woman, “like a beggar-woman,” and walks to the palace. Her veil falls amid the crowd, she enters like an ordinary maidservant without welcome, and, utterly exhausted and humiliated, finally collapses at Ramchandra’s feet.

After Surma’s death, the window in Udayaditya’s bedchamber symbolizes an absent home and his futile hope that Surma will return: he sits where she used to sit, looking out at the familiar moonlit garden and imagining her there. In prison, the small window instead becomes a symbol of freedom and hope. Through its view of the sky and flying birds, he can imagine his “cage” breaking and himself becoming free; away from it, he sees only darkness, making the bedchamber itself seem like a prison.

Sitaram’s dealings with Rukmini begin as a playful, flirtatious exchange built on money: he flatters her, borrows cash, and jokes about love while evading interest and repayment; she indulges him because of her attraction and confidence that she controls him. Their secret discussions later become tied to schemes involving Udayaditya. Once Udayaditya is imprisoned, however, Sitaram turns against Rukmini, blaming and threatening her for endangering him. She responds with murderous fury, claiming Udayaditya as her own and vowing revenge.

After helping fake Udayaditya’s death in the prison fire, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s house to steal her money, assuming she has died. He finds her alive, drenched, enraged, and seemingly returned from death. His attempts to revive their former playful intimacy only intensify her fury. She searches for a curved blade and attacks the place where he stood, forcing Sitaram to flee for his life. Fearing that she knows of his conspiracy and will expose him, he leaves Jessore with his family that same night.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction, drawing the guards and everyone else away so he can remove Udayaditya from prison. He then turns it into a deliberate cover-up: his men keep the blaze spreading and set fire to Udayaditya’s empty cell, while Sitaram plants bones, a skull, and the prince’s sword inside. He stages reports of screams and a collapsed roof, encouraging everyone to believe Udayaditya died in the fire. He also retrieves and destroys incriminating letters, intending to spread the death story and conceal the escape, though Rukmini ultimately exposes the deception.

He convinces himself that Udayaditya saved him only for the sake of his sister Vibha, not out of concern for Ramchandra himself. He regards the rescue as something Udayaditya was bound to do and later joins his courtiers in mocking him as Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya first dismisses the Emperor of Delhi’s anger as an empty threat, refusing to fear the soldiers it might bring. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram exploit that very fear by forging a petition bearing Udayaditya’s seal, supposedly accusing Pratapaditya of treason and appealing to the Emperor for the kingdom. Bhagavat presents it to Pratapaditya as proof that Udayaditya is sending a complaint to Delhi, turning the Emperor’s political threat into the pretext for imprisoning the prince.

Surma’s grooming of Vibha’s hair signifies their intimate bond and Surma’s caring presence: despite the Mahishi’s elaborate, imposed adornment, Vibha turns to Surma to make her hair as she likes. After Surma’s disappearance, Vibha waits for her to braid it, leaving it unbraided as she hopes Surma will return. Later, her unkempt hair becomes visible proof of Surma’s tragic absence and of Vibha’s neglect, loneliness, and sorrow in the palace.
